MSK–SKIN · MODULE II · HISTOLOGY & HISTOPATHOLOGY

Bone & Cartilage

From matrix chemistry and microscopic architecture to growth, remodeling, and clinical disease · based on the 55-page lecture packet and instructor handout

ObjectivesBig pictureBone structureMatrixCellsRemodelingCartilageDiseaseMasterStep 1

Learning objectives

  1. Define bone characteristics, function, bone classifications, and component parts.
  2. Identify bone-matrix components and relate each to the mechanical properties of bone.
  3. Recognize bone cells histologically and explain their functions and origins.
  4. Explain bone deposition, modeling, remodeling, resorption, and structural consequences.
  5. Compare hyaline, elastic, and fibrocartilage by composition, histology, location, and function.
  6. Recognize the histopathology of osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, osteomalacia, osteogenesis imperfecta, and Paget disease.

Big picture

Bone is a mineralized, vascular connective tissue that combines a stiff calcium-phosphate phase with a tough type I collagen scaffold. Osteoclasts remove bone; osteoblasts build it; osteocytes sense loads and coordinate turnover. Cartilage uses a hydrated, type II collagen–rich matrix to resist compression, but its avascularity limits healing.

MUST KNOW

One organizing question: Is the problem inadequate collagen, insufficient mineral, excessive or insufficient resorption, disorganized remodeling, or damaged cartilage? Each produces a different mechanical and microscopic pattern.

01 · Bone classes, macrostructure & microstructure

Why bone exists

Bone acts as a rigid lever for muscle-driven movement, protects organs, supports hematopoietic marrow, and stores approximately 99% of the body’s calcium. Shape helps predict mechanical role.

ClassExamplesFunctional interpretation
LongFemur, tibia, humerus, metacarpalsLeverage, load transmission
ShortCarpals, tarsalsSupport and controlled motion
FlatScapula, cranial bonesBroad muscle attachment and protection
IrregularVertebrae, sacrum, mandibleSpecialized load bearing/protection
SesamoidPatellaEmbedded in tendon; protects tendon and improves lever arm

Long and flat bones

Diaphysis = shaft with compact cortex surrounding medullary cavity; epiphysis = expanded end with internal trabeculae; metaphysis = transition; physis = hyaline cartilaginous growth plate, eventually replaced by a physeal scar. The outer bone surface is periosteal; the internal surface is endosteal. Flat bones contain outer and inner cortical tables around spongy diploë.

FeatureCortical / compactCancellous / trabecular
Adult skeletal mass~80%~20%
Surface-to-volume ratio2.520
Predominant siteShaft and outer shellMetaphyses/epiphyses and interior
Main roleMovement, support, protectionMultidirectional support and mineral homeostasis
Basic unitOsteonTrabecula

Read the microscopic architecture

An osteon contains concentric lamellae around a longitudinal Haversian canal for vessels and nerves. Transverse Volkmann canals connect vascular channels. Lacunae house osteocytes; canaliculi hold processes connecting them. Sharpey fibers anchor the periosteum to bone. The periosteum includes outer fibrous and inner osteogenic layers; the endosteum lines medullary and trabecular surfaces.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A ringed circle surrounds a central canal on a ground bone slide. What is it?
An osteon. The central opening is a Haversian canal; its concentric rings are lamellae. A Volkmann canal runs transversely to connect vascular channels.

02 · Bone matrix chemistry determines mechanical behavior

Wet-weight composition: ~60% hydroxyapatite mineral (Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂), ~30% organic matrix, ~10% water. Of the organic portion, ~90% is type I collagen and ~10% ground substance/noncollagenous proteins including osteocalcin. Mineral resists compression (stiffness); collagen resists tension (toughness). Together they make bone mechanically useful.

COMMON CONFUSION

Osteogenesis imperfecta: defective type I collagen → fragile organic scaffold. Osteomalacia: poorly mineralized osteoid → mechanically weak mineral phase. Both may fracture, but the defect is not the same.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

Lecture concept: defective mineralization vs type I collagen. First Aid adds: osteogenesis imperfecta is classically linked to blue sclerae, hearing loss and dentinogenesis imperfecta; osteomalacia/rickets is associated with defective mineralization, often vitamin D related. Why it matters: separate collagen disease from mineral disease in a vignette.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · If bone’s organic scaffold is normal but osteoid fails to mineralize, what disease pattern is suggested?
Osteomalacia (rickets in growing children). Increased unmineralized osteoid points to a mineralization problem, not primarily a type I collagen defect.

03 · Identify the four bone cell populations

The lineage distinction is fundamental: osteoclasts are hematopoietic/monocyte–macrophage lineage; osteoblasts, osteocytes, and bone lining cells derive from mesenchymal lineage.

CellAppearance / locationJob and stain
OsteoclastLarge, multinucleated; ruffled border in Howship lacunaResorbs mineral with acid; matrix with cathepsin K; TRAP+
OsteoblastCuboidal mononuclear row at surfaceProduces unmineralized osteoid and mineralization-associated proteins; alkaline phosphatase+
OsteocyteSmall, embedded in lacuna, processes in canaliculiMechanosenses, coordinates turnover; cannot undergo mitosis
Bone lining cellFlattened spindle-shaped surface cellBarrier and quiescent osteoblast progenitor

How osteoclasts resorb bone

Multiple precursors fuse. The cell seals to bone using integrin/osteopontin contacts, forms a ruffled border, releases protons to dissolve mineral, and secretes proteases (including cathepsin K) to degrade the organic matrix. M-CSF supports osteoclast precursors; RANKL binding RANK stimulates differentiation, fusion and activation. OPG is a decoy receptor that binds RANKL and opposes resorption.

How osteoblasts create bone

Osteoblasts deposit osteoid on a bone surface. Matrix vesicles and alkaline phosphatase help generate local phosphate so calcium phosphate precipitates as hydroxyapatite along collagen. Thus bone grows appositionally, not by mitosis of cells inside its rigid matrix. Vitamin D, PTH, calcitonin and FGF23 are systemic regulators shown in the lecture.

Osteocytes direct the response to loading

Osteocytes are former osteoblasts trapped in mineralized bone. Their dendritic processes extend through canaliculi and form gap-junction connections. Their signals include RANKL/M-CSF (promote osteoclasts), OPG (restrains osteoclasts), and sclerostin/Dkk1 (inhibit osteoblast-driven formation).

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which bone cell is multinucleated, TRAP positive, and derived from hematopoietic cells?
The osteoclast; it resorbs bone in Howship lacunae. Osteoblasts are mesenchymal and alkaline-phosphatase positive.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why can osteocytes coordinate a mechanically loaded region despite being embedded in mineral?
They detect mechanical conditions and signal along canalicular cellular processes and gap junctions to other osteocytes and surface bone cells.

04 · Deposition, modeling, remodeling and turnover

Modeling changes shape; remodeling renews tissue

Modeling: osteoclasts and osteoblasts work independently at different surfaces, changing diameter/shape during growth. Remodeling: their actions are coupled at one surface within a basic multicellular unit (BMU). Osteoclasts excavate; osteoblasts refill with osteoid that mineralizes. Coupled does not mean balanced: net loss or gain can result if the resorbed and replaced amounts differ.

In trabecular bone, BMUs work along existing trabecular surfaces (sometimes under a lining-cell canopy). In cortical bone, osteoclasts tunnel forward, then osteoblasts deposit concentric lamellae behind, leaving a central Haversian canal. Matrix-stored factors including TGF-β1 and IGF-1 can be released during resorption and help recruit osteoblasts to couple activity.

Balanced vs unbalanced remodeling

When resorption exceeds formation (for example, after menopause or in aging), bone mass can decrease. Drugs can shift this balance: lecture examples include antiresorptives bisphosphonates, SERMs, denosumab (anti-RANKL), and anabolic/osteogenic approaches teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumab (anti-sclerostin).

LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE

RANKL-driven osteoclast maturation → denosumab blocks RANKL → fewer active osteoclasts and less resorption. Sclerostin suppresses osteoblasts → anti-sclerostin therapy removes that brake on formation.

Structural quality and biomarkers

Immature woven bone has disorganized collagen and randomly distributed lacunae. Mature lamellar bone organizes collagen in alternating directions across adjacent lamellae. The lecturer discusses iliac crest biopsy and circulating turnover markers: resorption = type I collagen telopeptides/crosslinks and TRAP; formation = type I procollagen propeptides, osteocalcin and alkaline phosphatase.

MSK CONNECTION

Post-fracture woven bone must be remodeled into mechanically superior lamellar bone. Remodeling explains the transition from early repair to mature bone architecture.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A bone is losing mass despite osteoclasts and osteoblasts working in the same BMU. How is that possible?
Remodeling remains coupled in sequence but is quantitatively unbalanced: more matrix is removed than replaced.

05 · Cartilage composition, growth and three histologic types

Cartilage is avascular and aneural: chondrocytes depend on diffusion, which limits endogenous repair. All types have type II collagen fibrils and GAG-rich proteoglycan aggregates, with additional fibers distinguishing elastic cartilage and fibrocartilage.

Why cartilage resists compression

Proteoglycans such as aggrecan attach to hyaluronan. Negatively charged GAGs repel one another and recruit water, generating a hydrated gel that resists compression; the collagen network constrains swelling and provides tensile support. Cartilage has a large water fraction (roughly 60–80% shown in the lecture visual). Territorial matrix immediately near lacunae stains more basophilic because of GAG concentration; interterritorial matrix is lighter between groups.

Chondroblasts, chondrocytes and growth

Chondroblasts arise at the chondrogenic inner perichondrium and secrete type II collagen and proteoglycans. Once encased in their own matrix, they are chondrocytes in lacunae. Appositional growth adds layers at the perichondrial surface. Interstitial growth occurs when embedded chondrocytes divide and form isogenous/isogenic groups, crucial for growing cartilage under pressure. Perichondrium has outer fibrous and inner chondrogenic layers; it is absent on articular cartilage and growth plates, and fibrocartilage lacks perichondrium.

CartilageDistinctive matrix + histologyExamples / function
HyalineType II fibrils only; homogeneous glassy basophilic matrix; no visible collagen fibers by light microscopyTrachea, articular surface, costal cartilage, physis; smooth articulation and growth
ElasticType II plus visible elastic fibers; more chondrocytes; springs back after bendingAuricle, epiglottis, auditory tube; flexible support
FibrocartilageType II fibrils plus thick type I fibers; chondrocytes arranged in rows; no perichondriumMeniscus, intervertebral disc, pubic symphysis; resists tension and compression

EXAM TRAP

Invisible fibers in hyaline cartilage ≠ no collagen. Type II fibrils are too small and share the refractive index of ground substance; fibrocartilage has visible type I bundles.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which cartilage shows rows of chondrocytes interspersed with thick eosinophilic collagen and lacks perichondrium?
Fibrocartilage: abundant type I fiber bundles, in addition to type II fibrils.

06 · Histopathology and clinical applications

Recognize disease from which phase or process is disrupted before memorizing its name.

DisorderPrimary lesion / characteristic pathologyReasoning clue
OsteoporosisLow bone mass and compromised trabecular architecture; resorption outstrips formationFragility despite ordinarily mineralized remaining matrix
Osteomalacia / ricketsExcess unmineralized osteoidDefective mineralization, often vitamin D related
Osteogenesis imperfectaType I collagen abnormality; fracture-prone boneOrganic scaffold / tensile toughness defect
Paget diseaseFocal, markedly elevated disorganized resorption and formation; woven and lamellar mosaicLarge/many osteoclasts and chaotic remodeling
OsteoarthritisFibrillation, wear and loss of articular hyaline cartilagePoor repair because cartilage is avascular
Osteopetrosis (comparison)Defective osteoclast resorption; dense yet fracture-prone bone; narrowing of medullary spacesToo little bone resorption, not too little bone formation

Osteoclast activity is not the same as bone quality

Osteoporosis in this lecture is associated with excessive net resorption; osteopetrosis instead involves inadequate osteoclastic removal. Both can cause fractures, although the latter can appear abnormally dense. In Paget disease, focal excessive resorption is followed by excessive but disorganized formation, creating a structurally unsound mosaic.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

Lecture concept: Paget disease has disordered focal remodeling. First Aid adds: a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone and elevated alkaline phosphatase are classic clues; skull involvement may cause hearing symptoms. Why it matters: high turnover does not guarantee strong bone.

Clinical connection: microfracture surgery

The lecture describes cartilage debridement followed by small holes into subchondral bone, allowing marrow-derived cells to populate a clot and generate fibrocartilage. The replacement is not mechanically identical to native articular hyaline cartilage. The lecture cites a 66% long-term failure rate and a mean time to failure of approximately four years for the discussed study—these are study-specific figures, not universal outcomes.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

Lecture concept: OA damages articular cartilage. First Aid adds: joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis are commonly tested OA imaging associations. Why it matters: connect cartilage loss to a radiographic joint disease pattern.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why can osteopetrosis and osteoporosis both result in fractures?
Osteopetrosis accumulates poorly remodeled dense bone because osteoclast function is impaired; osteoporosis loses bone architecture when resorption exceeds formation. Density alone is not mechanical quality.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Microfracture can fill a cartilage defect. Why might the repair later fail?
It typically creates fibrocartilage rather than durable native articular hyaline cartilage, so its mechanical response to repeated loading is inferior.

Master these before moving on

Material strength has two phases

Hydroxyapatite provides compression resistance; type I collagen provides tensile toughness. This underpins the distinction between osteomalacia and osteogenesis imperfecta.

Lineage predicts cell function

Osteoclasts are hematopoietic and remove bone; osteoblasts, osteocytes and lining cells come from mesenchymal lineage. This organizes staining and pathology.

Coupling ≠ balance

Remodeling pairs resorption with formation on the same surface, but the amounts can differ. This explains net skeletal gain/loss and drug mechanisms.

Cartilage is hydrated and avascular

GAG-bound water underlies compression resistance, while limited nutrient delivery explains poor repair.

See tissue patterns, not just names

Osteon lamellae, osteoclast lacunae, cartilage cell rows, osteoid seams and Paget mosaic are practical identification anchors.

The most useful First Aid connections

  1. OI: type I collagen defect → recurrent fractures; blue sclerae/hearing/dental findings add recognition value.
  2. Osteomalacia: defective mineralization → increased osteoid; evaluate vitamin D/calcium/phosphate context.
  3. Paget: high-turnover mosaic bone → classic alkaline phosphatase association.
  4. RANKL: osteoclast maturation axis → denosumab mechanism.
  5. OA: articular cartilage loss → joint-space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis.

Source distinction: these are selective board associations; do not mistake them for additional lecture learning objectives.
